samples.text:
In many towns, the small shops are closing and large supermarkets and shopping centres are taking their place. In my opinion, this change has some advantages, but the disadvantages are more serious.

To begin with, there are some benefits of supermarkets. They are usually cheaper than small shops because they buy products in large quantity. This is important for families who have a low income. Also, supermarkets are very convenient, because customers can buy everything they need in one place, such as food, clothes and electronic, and they can park their car easily. Many of them are open for long hours, so people who works late can still do their shopping.

However, I think the disadvantages are more important. When small shops close, the owners lose their business and many local people lose their jobs. The money which people spend in supermarkets often goes to big companies in other cities, not to the local community. Moreover, the town centre become less attractive, because there are many empty shops and fewer people walking in the streets. Small shops also give a personal service. The shopkeeper knows his customers and can give them advices, but in a big supermarket nobody knows you. Finally, old people who cannot drive find it difficult to go to shopping centres outside the town.

In conclusion, supermarkets and shopping centres are cheap and convenient, but they damage local businesses and change the character of towns. For these reasons, I believe that the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, and local governments should help small shops to survive.
samples.why: Clear position with a judgement · relevant ideas on both sides, some only briefly developed · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · word-form, agreement and countability errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Across many towns, independent shops are gradually disappearing as large supermarkets and out-of-town shopping centres take over. Although this development offers consumers some clear benefits, I believe the loss to local communities is greater.

It is true that large retailers bring certain advantages. Because they buy goods in enormous quantities, they can offer lower prices than small shops, which is especially important for households on tight budget. They also provide convenience: shoppers can buy groceries, clothing and household items under one roof, often late into the evening and with free parking. In addition, supermarkets tend to offer a much wider range of products, including foreign foods that small local stores would rarely stock.

Nevertheless, the disadvantages are more far-reaching. When independent businesses close, the effect goes beyond the owners themselves. High streets that were once busy become lined with empty premises, which makes town centres less attractive and can even encourage vandalism. More of the money spent also leaves the area, as profits go to national chains rather than circulating among local families. Moreover, small shops often play a social role that supermarkets cannot replace; a local grocer who greets customers by name offers a sense of connection that is particularly valuable for elderly people living alone. Finally, shopping centres built on the edge of town encourage car use, which increases traffic and puts residents without transport at a disadvantage.

In conclusion, supermarkets and shopping centres undoubtedly make shopping cheaper and more convenient. However, since they weaken local economies, damage town centres and reduce community life, I believe that on balance their disadvantages outweigh their advantages.
samples.why: Clear position maintained · advantages acknowledged and disadvantages extended with relevant support · logical organisation with a range of linkers · good collocation (under one roof, far-reaching) · one article slip.

samples.text:
The decline of the independent high-street shop in the face of competition from supermarkets and shopping centres is a familiar story in many towns. While the change has undoubtedly benefited shoppers in certain respects, I would argue that, taken as a whole, its advantages are outweighed by its costs.

The case for large retailers rests largely on price and convenience. Economies of scale allow supermarkets to negotiate lower prices from suppliers and pass at least some of these savings on to customers, which matters considerably to families whose budgets are stretched. Their extended opening hours, extensive product ranges and ample parking also suit modern lifestyles, in which many people have little time to visit several separate shops. For consumers, then, the immediate benefits are tangible.

The disadvantages, however, are broader and longer-lasting. Independent shops are typically owned by local residents, so the money spent in them tends to circulate within the community, supporting other local businesses and jobs. When they are replaced by national chains, a greater share of that spending is channelled elsewhere. The physical fabric of towns suffers too: once enough shops close, footfall declines, remaining businesses struggle and high streets can enter a spiral of decline marked by vacant units. There is also a social dimension that is easily overlooked. Small shops often serve as informal meeting points where neighbours exchange news, and for older or less mobile residents, a daily visit to a nearby store may be an important source of human contact. Out-of-town shopping centres, by contrast, are designed around the car and can leave such people isolated.

In conclusion, supermarkets and shopping centres offer genuine savings and convenience, but these gains are largely private and short-term, whereas the erosion of local economies and community life affects entire towns. For this reason, I believe the disadvantages outweigh the advantages.
samples.why: Clear, well-reasoned judgement · ideas fully extended with precise supporting detail · logical sequencing and skilful cohesion · wide, idiomatic vocabulary (economies of scale, footfall) · wide range of accurate structures.
